steps.prompt: What happens to the verb after he, she and it?
steps.why: After he, she and it, the verb takes -s.
steps.html:
I get up early. — He gets up early.

We watch the penguins. — She watches the penguins.

They go to bed late. — He goes to bed late.

steps.title: Present Simple · positive
steps.html:
PersonVerbExample
I / You / We / Theybase formThey work on the island.
He / She / It+ -sHe works on the island.
-ch, -sh, -s, -x+ -esShe watches the birds.
go, do+ -esHe goes home. She does the shopping.
have→ hasHe has lunch at one.

Use the Present Simple for what is true every day, not just today.

Only he, she and it take the -s. Everyone else uses the base form.

Learners often drop the -s. He work here is one of the most common A1 mistakes.

The negative comes in Lesson 8.

steps.title: Adverbs of frequency
steps.html:
How oftenWhere it goesExample
always, usually, oftenbefore the main verbHe always gets up early.
sometimes, hardly ever, neverbefore the main verbShe never works alone.
with to beafter am / is / areHis work is sometimes dangerous.
once / twice a weekat the endI see friends twice a week.

The frequency word goes before the verb — but after is, am and are.

never is already negative. Do not add another negative word.

steps.title: The day I would live again
steps.html:
Amina, 34. My perfect day is a Saturday. I get up late — about ten — and I make breakfast for everybody. Then we walk to the market. I never look at my phone on a Saturday. In the evening my sister comes and we watch an old film together.

Deniz, 51. I am a baker, so my perfect day starts at four in the morning. That sounds terrible, but the town is quiet and the bread is warm. I finish at one, I have lunch with my wife, and then I sleep for an hour. I hardly ever go out in the evening.

Kostya, 22. My perfect day is a day with no plan. I usually listen to music, I sometimes see friends, and I always end the day in the same place: a small café near my flat. The coffee there is not very good, but the people are.
